title: Boring or Bored
overview: This unit is about how a thing is, and how that thing makes you feel. The work was tiring, and you were tired. You also learn the order of describing words, and how much of a quality there is. At the end you give an opinion and a reason for it.
learningPath: Lesson: hear the -ing word and the -ed word side by side.
Words: four groups, thirty-three words for feelings, things and amounts.
Pattern 1: boring or bored, the thing or the person.
Pattern 2: a small old wooden box, in that order.
Pattern 3: too hot, quite hot, not hot enough.
Pattern 4: good at, keen on, afraid of.
Reading: three texts, then nine questions with answers.
Speaking, writing, quiz, then the assignment.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 9.
This unit is about two words that look the same and are not.
Listen to these two sentences.
The film was boring.
I was bored.
Both words come from one verb.
One ends in -ing. One ends in -ed.
The -ing word is about the thing.
The film, the book, the work, the day.
The thing does it to you.
The -ed word is about the person.
I was bored. She was bored. They were bored.
The person feels it.
So ask yourself one question.
Am I talking about the thing, or about the person?
The thing takes -ing. The person takes -ed.
Here are more pairs.
The lesson is interesting. I am interested.
The form is confusing. I am confused.
The news is exciting. We are excited.
The work is tiring. He is tired.
Now say this out loud.
I am boring.
That is correct English, but it may not be what you mean.
It says that other people are bored when they listen to you.
If you mean the day was long and slow, say I am bored.
This is the commonest mistake in this unit.
You can catch it alone.
Look at the word in front of the -ing or the -ed word.
If it is a thing, use -ing. If it is a person, use -ed.
Now the second pattern.
English puts describing words in one order.
Size first. Then age. Then shape. Then colour. Then what it is made of.
A small old wooden box.
A large white plastic bowl.
A long narrow metal shelf.
You do not say a wooden small old box.
Nobody will correct you, so learn the line by heart.
Size, age, shape, colour, what it is made of.
Now the third pattern.
Sometimes you want to say how much of a quality there is.
The tea is hot. That is all you say.
The tea is quite hot. That is a good amount.
The tea is rather hot. That is more than you wanted.
The tea is too hot. Now you cannot drink it.
The tea is not hot enough. Now there is too little heat.
Too comes in front of the describing word.
Enough comes after it.
We say not warm enough. We do not say not enough warm.
There are more of these words in this unit.
Extremely, slightly, hardly, almost, completely.
The room was extremely cold. That is a very great amount.
The room was slightly cold. That is a very little.
I hardly slept. That is almost no sleep.
The work is almost finished. A little is left.
The work is completely finished. Nothing is left.
Now the fourth pattern.
Some describing words always bring a small word with them.
Good at. Interested in. Afraid of.
The small word never changes.
We say good at English, never good in English.
We say interested in music, never interested for music.
Here are the ones in this unit.
Keen on. Fond of. Aware of. Ashamed of.
Grateful for. Curious about. Nervous about. Impatient with.
Learn the two words together, as if they were one.
The words of this unit come in four groups.
How a thing makes you feel. What a thing is like.
How much of it there is. How you are about it.
In every task you may invent the person, the job and the place.
Now start with the words, then the four patterns.
Say every example out loud once before you write it.

words.meaning: A thing is interesting when it makes you want to know more.
practice: That book is interesting, so I read it twice.
The most interesting part was at the end.
Was the film interesting?
An old building is more interesting than a new one.
words.starter: The most interesting thing in my week was ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with interesting about things, and stop me if I use it about a person who feels it.

words.meaning: You are interested when you want to know more about something.
words.example: I am interested in old buildings.
practice: She is interested in music and she sings every week.
He was interested, so he asked two questions.
Are you interested in this kind of work?
I am not interested in football.
words.starter: I am interested in ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between interesting and interested, and give me one sentence of each to correct.

words.meaning: You are bored when nothing around you is interesting.
words.example: I was bored on the long journey.
practice: The shop was quiet all day and I was bored.
A bored person looks at the clock.
Were you bored in the second hour?
He is never bored, because he always has a book.
words.starter: I am bored when ...
words.tutor: Ask me for two sentences with bored and two with boring, then tell me which word goes with a person.

words.meaning: A thing is confusing when it is hard to understand.
practice: The map was confusing, so we asked at the shop.
Small writing on a long form is confusing.
Why is this page so confusing?
The first part was clear and the second part was confusing.
words.starter: One confusing thing in English is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a confusing form in four sentences, and check that I use confusing about the paper and confused about the person.

words.meaning: You are confused when you cannot understand something.
words.example: I was confused by the map.
practice: After ten minutes we were both confused.
She looked confused, so I told her again slowly.
Are you confused about the time?
I am confused, because the notice says two different things.
words.starter: I was confused when ...
words.tutor: Ask me three questions about a confusing notice and let me answer with confused each time.

words.meaning: A thing is exciting when it makes you feel happy and wide awake.
practice: A new job is exciting and a little frightening.
The last ten minutes of the game were exciting.
Is a long journey exciting for you?
My neighbour said the film was exciting, but it was slow.
words.starter: The most exciting day of my year was ...
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with exciting, and make one of them a question.

words.meaning: You are excited when you want something to happen and you cannot wait.
words.example: She was excited about the trip.
practice: We are excited, because the shop opens on Monday.
He was too excited to eat his breakfast.
Are you excited about the weekend?
The children were excited and nobody was quiet.
words.starter: I am excited about ...
words.tutor: Ask me which small word comes after excited, then give me two sentences to finish with it.

words.meaning: A thing is frightening when it makes you afraid.
practice: The road was narrow and the traffic was frightening.
A frightening story is hard to forget.
Was the accident frightening?
Speaking in front of twenty people is frightening at first.
words.starter: One frightening thing for me is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with frightening about things, and one with frightened about a person.

words.meaning: Made from a tree.
practice: I keep my keys in a small wooden box.
A wooden spoon is light and warm to hold.
Is the door wooden or metal?
The old wooden shelf is rough on one side.
words.starter: One wooden thing in this room is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to describe three wooden things, each one with a size word in front of wooden.

words.meaning: Made of the same hard, heavy material as a key or a spoon.
practice: A metal key does not break easily.
She put the hot pan on a metal tray.
Is that bowl metal or plastic?
The long narrow metal shelf holds twelve books.
words.starter: One metal thing I use every day is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with metal, and check that metal comes just in front of the thing.

words.meaning: Made of a light, cheap material that does not break when it falls.
practice: I carry water in a large plastic bottle.
A plastic bowl is lighter than a metal one.
Are these plates plastic?
The old plastic chair is not strong enough for me.
words.starter: One plastic thing in my bag is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to compare a plastic bottle and a metal bottle in three sentences.

words.meaning: With the shape of a plate or a clock.
practice: We eat at a small round table in the kitchen.
A clock is round and a window is often square.
Is the plate round?
She gave me a big round metal tray.
words.starter: One round thing near me is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to name four round things and put a size word in front of each one.

words.meaning: With four sides of the same length.
practice: The card is square and white.
A square box is easy to carry.
Is this table square or round?
The old square wooden door is very heavy.
words.starter: One square thing in this room is ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between round and square, with one example of each.

words.meaning: Not wide. Only a short way from one side to the other.
practice: The shelf is too narrow for this box.
We walked along a narrow road with no pavement.
Is the door wide enough, or is it narrow?
A narrow bridge is slow for two cars.
words.starter: One narrow place near my home is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with narrow and one with wide, so I can hear the difference.

words.meaning: Flat and soft when you touch it, with nothing rough on it.
practice: Your hand moves easily over a smooth table.
The paper is smooth on one side.
Is this wall smooth or rough?
They made the rough piece of wood smooth again.
words.starter: One smooth thing I can touch now is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to describe two things I can touch, one smooth and one rough.

words.meaning: Not smooth. It is not flat, and your hand feels it.
practice: The road is rough after the storm.
A rough shelf can hurt your hand.
Why is this side rough?
The wooden box was rough, so I worked on it for an hour.
words.starter: One rough thing near me is ...
words.tutor: Ask me four questions with rough and smooth about things in a kitchen.

words.meaning: Bright, because the light comes back off it.
practice: She gave me a shiny metal key.
The floor is shiny after you wash it.
Is the new bowl shiny?
A shiny plate looks clean even when it is old.
words.starter: One shiny thing in this room is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to describe a shiny thing in three sentences, and check I do not say shining.

words.meaning: A good amount, but not the most.
practice: The work was quite hard, but I finished it.
It is quite late, so I will go home.
Is the shop quite near?
She is quite good at numbers.
words.starter: My day today was quite ...
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with quite, and tell me if any of them should use rather instead.

words.meaning: More than you want, or more than you expected.
practice: The film was rather slow and I turned it off.
This glass is rather dirty. Please wash it again.
Is the road rather narrow here?
The room was rather cold last night.
words.starter: One thing today was rather ...
words.tutor: Ask me whether quite and rather mean the same thing, and give me one sentence that shows they do not.

words.meaning: As much as you need. It comes after the describing word.
words.example: The room is not warm enough.
practice: This shelf is not wide enough for the box.
Is the tea cool enough to drink?
One hour is not enough for this work.
The bag is big enough for all of it.
words.starter: One thing in my day is not long enough, and it is ...
words.tutor: Ask me where enough goes in a sentence, then give me three sentences with it in the wrong place.

words.meaning: Very, very much.
practice: He was extremely kind and he waited with us.
The second session was extremely busy.
Was the journey extremely long?
This box is extremely heavy for one person.
words.starter: One thing that is extremely important to me is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with extremely and three with slightly, so I can hear the two ends.

words.meaning: A very little.
practice: The door is slightly open.
I am slightly tired, but I can work.
Is the second box slightly bigger?
The water is slightly warm, not hot.
words.starter: One thing that is slightly different today is ...
words.tutor: Ask me to put slightly into four sentences, and check that it goes in front of the describing word.

words.meaning: Almost not at all.
practice: She hardly ate anything at breakfast.
The shop was so quiet that we hardly worked.
Can you hardly hear me?
He hardly ever comes on a Monday.
words.starter: Yesterday I hardly ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with hardly, then ask me whether hardly means a lot or almost none.

words.meaning: Very near to it, but not all the way.
practice: It is almost four o'clock.
The bottle is almost empty.
Are you almost ready?
Almost every shop on this street is shut on Sunday.
words.starter: I have almost finished ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between almost finished and completely finished, with one example of each.

words.meaning: All of it, with nothing left.
practice: The bottle is completely empty.
I was completely confused by that form.
Is the room completely clean now?
She was completely right about the price.
words.starter: One thing I have completely finished is ...
words.tutor: Ask me for four sentences with completely, and tell me if any of them should be almost instead.

words.meaning: Feeling bad about something you did. It takes of.
words.example: He was ashamed of the mistake.
practice: I am not ashamed of my English.
She was ashamed of nothing, because she had done her best.
Are you ashamed of that old photo?
Nobody should be ashamed of asking a question.
words.starter: Nobody should be ashamed of ...
words.tutor: Ask me which small word comes after ashamed, then give me two sentences to finish.

words.meaning: Not able to wait quietly. It takes with.
words.example: The driver was impatient with the traffic.
practice: Do not be impatient with yourself when you learn.
He was impatient, so he asked the same question twice.
Are you impatient with slow work?
The queue was long and everybody was impatient.
words.starter: I am impatient when ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with impatient, and check that I use with when I name a person.

words.meaning: Wanting to do something very much. It takes on.
practice: I am keen on this kind of work.
She is not keen on long meetings.
Are you keen on the idea?
He is keen on getting better at numbers.
words.starter: I am keen on ...
words.tutor: Ask me what comes after keen, and give me one sentence with a verb after it.

words.meaning: Liking somebody or something for a long time. It takes of.
words.example: I am fond of that old wooden chair.
practice: She is fond of her neighbours.
I am not fond of sitting for an hour.
Are you fond of this city?
He is fond of the shop on the corner.
words.starter: I am fond of ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between fond of and keen on, with one example of each.

words.meaning: Knowing that something is there or is true. It takes of.
words.example: He is aware of the rule.
practice: I was not aware of the change in the time.
Are you aware of the notice on the door?
She is aware of every price in the shop.
Be aware of the step at the corner.
words.starter: I am aware of ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with aware of, and one question with it.

words.meaning: Feeling thanks to somebody who helped you. It takes for.
words.example: I am grateful for your help.
practice: She was grateful for the call from the office.
We are grateful for every quiet hour.
Are you grateful for the help you got?
I am grateful for this job, even on a hard day.
words.starter: I am grateful for ...
words.tutor: Ask me which small word follows grateful, then let me thank you for three different things.

words.meaning: Wanting to know about something. It takes about.
words.example: I am curious about the new shop.
practice: She is curious about other people's work.
He was curious, so he read the whole notice.
Are you curious about the answer?
I am curious about how this machine works.
words.starter: I am curious about ...
words.tutor: Ask me the difference between curious and interested, with one sentence of each.

words.meaning: A little afraid before something happens. It takes about.
words.example: I am nervous about the test tomorrow.
practice: She was nervous about speaking in front of ten people.
He is nervous, but he is going anyway.
Are you nervous about the first day?
Everybody is nervous about a new job at first.
words.starter: I am nervous about ...
words.tutor: Ask me for three sentences with nervous about, and tell me if I say nervous of by mistake.

grammar.title: Boring or Bored
grammar.explanation: Two words come from one verb. The -ing word describes the thing. The -ed word describes the person who feels it. The film was boring, so I was bored. Ask one question: am I talking about the thing, or about the person?
grammar.rule:
the thing takes -ing
The film was boring.
The form is confusing.
The news is exciting.
The storm was frightening.
The work is tiring.

the person takes -ed
I was bored.
I am confused.
We are excited.
She was frightened.
He is tired.

the two words side by side
The lesson is interesting. I am interested.
The map was confusing. I was confused.
The trip is exciting. They are excited.

a small word often follows the -ed word
interested in, excited about, confused by, bored with
I am interested in old buildings.
She is excited about the trip.

I am boring is correct English
It says that other people are bored when they listen to you.
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
The facts: you filled in a long form. You could not understand it.
Step 1. Write two sentences. One about the form, one about you.
Step 2. The form is a thing, so it takes -ing.
Sentence 1: The form was confusing.
Step 3. You are a person, so you take -ed.
Sentence 2: I was confused.
Step 4. Join them with so.
Answer: The form was confusing, so I was confused.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to say I am boring when you mean I am bored. I am boring says that other people are bored with you. A person takes -ed: I am bored.
grammar.tip: The thing does it. The person feels it.
grammar.practice:
Write the right word.
1. The journey was long and slow. I was (boring, bored).
2. That book is (interesting, interested). I read it twice.
3. She is (exciting, excited) about the new job.
4. The map was (confusing, confused), so we asked at the shop.
5. The storm last night was (frightening, frightened).
6. He works twelve hours a day, so he is always (tiring, tired).
7. Now write two sentences about one thing. Use an -ing word in the first and an -ed word in the second.
grammar.answers:
1. bored  2. interesting  3. excited  4. confusing  5. frightening  6. tired
Item 7 is your own writing, so there is no fixed answer. Model: The lesson was interesting, so I was interested.
The likeliest wrong answer is item 4. The map is a thing, not a person, so it takes -ing. You were the one who was confused.
Item 6 catches people too. He is the person, so the word is tired. The work is the thing, and the work is tiring.

grammar.title: A Small Old Wooden Box
grammar.explanation: English puts describing words in one order in front of the thing. Size comes first, then age, then shape, then colour, then what it is made of. Words like smooth, rough and shiny go in front of all of them.
grammar.rule:
size, age, shape, colour, material
a small old wooden box
a large white plastic bowl
a long narrow metal shelf
a big round green plate

one word from each group, never two from the same group
a small wooden chair
a round metal tray
a narrow plastic bin

smooth, rough and shiny go in front
a shiny metal spoon
a rough old wall

not the other way round
We do not say a wooden small box.

two describing words after is, joined by and
The box is small and old.
The plate is round and green.
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
The thing: a box. It is small. It is old. It is made from a tree.
Step 1. Say the order out loud: size, age, shape, colour, material.
Step 2. Small is a size, so it goes first.
Step 3. Old is an age, so it goes second.
Step 4. Wooden says what it is made of, so it goes last, next to the box.
Answer: a small old wooden box.
Now say the same thing after is.
Answer: The box is small and old, and it is wooden.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to put the material first: a wooden small box. What a thing is made of always goes last, next to the thing: a small wooden box.
grammar.tip: Size, age, shape, colour, material. The material sits closest to the thing.
grammar.practice:
Put the words in the right order.
1. (metal, narrow) a ... shelf
2. (old, plastic) an ... chair
3. (round, small) a ... table
4. (new, metal, big) a ... key
5. (square, wooden, old) a ... door
6. (white, plastic, large) a ... bowl
7. Now write one sentence about something you can see, with two describing words in front of it.
grammar.answers:
1. a narrow metal shelf  2. an old plastic chair  3. a small round table  4. a big new metal key  5. an old square wooden door  6. a large white plastic bowl
Item 7 is your own writing. Model: I can see a small round metal tray.
The likeliest wrong answer is item 5. Wooden says what the door is made of, so it comes last: an old square wooden door.
Item 2 catches people for another reason. It is an old plastic chair, not a old plastic chair, because old begins with a vowel sound.

grammar.title: Too Hot, Quite Hot, Not Hot Enough
grammar.explanation: These words say how much of a quality there is. Quite is a good amount and rather is more than you wanted. Too is more than you can use. Not enough is less than you need. Too goes in front of the describing word, and enough goes after it.
grammar.rule:
how much, from a very little to all of it
slightly cold is a very little
quite cold is a good amount
rather cold is more than you wanted
extremely cold is a very great amount
completely cold is all of it

too goes in front of the describing word
The tea is too hot to drink.
This shelf is too narrow for the box.

enough goes after the describing word
The room is not warm enough.
Is the shelf wide enough?
We do not say not enough warm.

hardly means almost not at all
I hardly slept last night.
She hardly ate anything.

almost means very near, but not all the way
The work is almost finished.
It is almost four o'clock.
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
The facts: the tea is very hot. You cannot drink it yet.
Step 1. Ask whether this is a good amount of heat or more than you can use.
Step 2. You cannot drink it, so it is more than you can use.
Step 3. The word for that is too, and too goes in front of hot.
Answer: The tea is too hot.
Now say the same thing from the other side.
Answer: The tea is not cool enough to drink.
Enough goes after the describing word, never in front of it.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to put enough in front of the word: the room is not enough warm. Enough always comes after the describing word: the room is not warm enough.
grammar.tip: Too comes before. Enough comes after. Quite is fine, rather is a little too much.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right word.
1. The soup is (quite, too) hot to eat. I will wait ten minutes.
2. I (hardly, almost) slept last night, so I am very tired today.
3. The work is (almost, completely) finished. One box is still open.
4. The bottle is (slightly, extremely) heavy. I can carry it easily.
5. The glass is (rather, hardly) dirty. Please wash it again.
6. The room is not warm (enough, too).
Now finish these two sentences.
7. The shelf is not wide ... . The box will not go on it.
8. The film was ... slow, so I turned it off after twenty minutes.
grammar.answers:
1. too  2. hardly  3. almost  4. slightly  5. rather  6. enough  7. enough
Item 8 is your own choice. Rather or extremely both work. Model: The film was rather slow, so I turned it off after twenty minutes.
Item 4 is the one people miss. Extremely heavy means you could not carry it easily, so slightly is the word that fits the second sentence.
Items 6 and 7 make the same point. We say not warm enough and not wide enough, never not enough warm.

grammar.title: Good At, Interested In, Afraid Of
grammar.explanation: Some describing words always bring one small word with them. The small word never changes, and you cannot guess it. We say good at English, never good in English. Learn the two words together, as if they were one.
grammar.rule:
at
good at, bad at
I am good at fixing things.

in
interested in
She is interested in old buildings.

of
afraid of, fond of, aware of, ashamed of, full of
I am fond of that old chair.
He is aware of the rule.

on
keen on
They are keen on walking.

for
grateful for, ready for, late for
I am grateful for your help.

about
curious about, nervous about, excited about, worried about
I am nervous about the test.

with
impatient with, happy with, busy with
Do not be impatient with yourself.

after the small word, a verb takes -ing
good at fixing, keen on walking, afraid of falling
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
You want to say that you like walking and you do it often.
Step 1. Choose the describing word. Keen fits.
Step 2. Keen always brings on with it.
Step 3. After on, a verb takes -ing, so walk becomes walking.
Answer: I am keen on walking.
Now say the same idea with fond.
Fond brings of, so the answer is: I am fond of walking.
The describing word chooses the small word. Learn the pair.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to use in after good: I am good in English. Good always brings at with it: I am good at English.
grammar.tip: Learn good at as one piece, not as two words.
grammar.practice:
Write the right small word: at, in, of, on, for, about or with.
1. She is very good ... numbers.
2. I am interested ... old buildings.
3. He is afraid ... dogs.
4. They are keen ... walking in the morning.
5. I am grateful ... your help.
6. We are curious ... the new shop on the corner.
7. Do not be impatient ... yourself.
8. I am fond ... that old wooden chair.
grammar.answers:
1. at  2. in  3. of  4. on  5. for  6. about  7. with  8. of
Eight out of eight means you have it. Six or seven means write the pairs in a list and say them out loud twice.
The likeliest wrong answer is item 1. Good always brings at, never in: good at numbers.
Item 7 catches people too. Impatient brings with when you name a person: impatient with yourself.

readings.title: A Long Day and a Short Film
readings.setting: A shop during the day, and a flat in the evening
readings.passage:
I work in a shop, and yesterday was a long day.
The shop was quiet from nine until four.
Nobody came in, and I had nothing to do.
I was bored. Extremely bored.
A quiet shop is boring, and a bored person looks at the clock.
In the afternoon a woman came in with a form.
She wanted help with it, and the form was confusing.
It had six pages and very small writing.
We read it together, and after ten minutes we were both confused.
In the end I called the office, and a man there told us what to write.
He was extremely kind, and he was not impatient with us.
I was grateful for that call.
In the evening I watched a film at home.
My neighbour told me it was exciting.
It was not exciting. It was rather slow.
After twenty minutes I was bored again, so I turned it off.
Here is the strange part of the day.
The same day gave me one boring hour and one interesting hour.
The quiet shop was boring. The confusing form was interesting.
I did not want that form, but I learned something from it.
Now I am curious about forms.
I am not good at them yet, but I am keen on getting better.
A boring day can still teach you something.

readings.title: What Is It Made Of?
readings.setting: A general page about everyday things, not about any one person
readings.passage:
Look at the things around you now.
Every one of them is made of something.
Most everyday things are made from a tree, from metal or from plastic.
A wooden thing comes from a tree. A wooden spoon is light and warm to hold.
A metal thing is heavy and hard. A metal key does not break easily.
A plastic thing is light and cheap. A plastic bottle does not break when it falls.
Things also have a shape.
A plate is round. A window is often square.
A shelf is long and narrow.
Things feel different when you touch them.
A new plate is smooth. Your hand moves easily over it.
An old wall is rough. It is not flat, and your hand feels every part of it.
A clean knife is shiny, because the light comes back off it.
Now put two of these words together in front of the thing.
English has an order for them, and it almost never changes.
Size comes first. Then age. Then shape. Then colour.
Last of all comes the material, which means what the thing is made of.
A small old wooden box. A large white plastic bowl.
A long narrow metal shelf. A big round green plate.
You can hear the order when you read the words out loud.
A wooden small box sounds wrong in English, and now you know why.
When you describe a thing, ask three questions.
How big is it? What shape is it? What is it made of?
Answer them in that order and the sentence will be right.

readings.title: Notice Board at the Library
readings.setting: The board beside the door of a small library
readings.passage:
LIBRARY NOTICE BOARD
MAKE IT AND MEND IT: FREE SATURDAY SESSIONS

Three sessions. A session is one hour of work together.
You can come to one, to two, or to all three. They are free.

10.00 SESSION 1: WOOD
Bring an old wooden chair or a small wooden box.
We show you how to make a rough piece of wood smooth again.
This session is quiet and it is slow.

12.00 SESSION 2: METAL AND PLASTIC
Bring a metal spoon, a plastic bowl or an old key.
This session is short. It is extremely busy and rather loud.

14.00 SESSION 3: TALK
One hour. Somebody talks about the things people made at home a hundred years ago.
There are no tools in this session. You sit and you listen.

WHAT TO BRING
One thing to work on. Nothing else. We have all the tools here.
The room is not large enough for a big table.

TO ASK A QUESTION
Call 555 0164, Monday to Friday, from 10 until 4.

WHAT PEOPLE SAID LAST MONTH
"I am not good at making things, and I was nervous about coming. Everybody was kind. I am keen on Session 1 again."
From a tenant in Block D.

"Session 2 was extremely interesting, but it was too short. One hour is not enough."
From a driver.

"I was bored in Session 3. The talk was slow, and I am not fond of sitting for an hour. My friend loved it."
From a student.

comprehension.q: Why was the writer bored at work?
comprehension.a: Because the shop was quiet, nobody came in, and there was nothing to do.
comprehension.why: The first four lines give all three facts, one after the other.

comprehension.q: The writer says the form was confusing. Who was confused?
comprehension.a: The writer and the woman who brought the form.
comprehension.why: The form is the thing, so it is confusing. The two people are the ones who feel it, and the text says they were both confused.

comprehension.q: The writer says the film was rather slow. What does rather tell you here?
comprehension.a: That the film was more slow than the writer wanted.
comprehension.why: Rather says there is more of a quality than you want. Quite would have meant a good amount, and the writer turned the film off.

comprehension.q: Does the writer think a boring day is a bad day? How do you know?
comprehension.a: No. The last line says a boring day can still teach you something.
comprehension.why: The writer learned about forms from the hour that was not boring, and then says so in the last line.

comprehension.q: In what order does English put describing words in front of a thing?
comprehension.a: Size, then age, then shape, then colour, then what it is made of.
comprehension.why: The text gives the five in that order, and then gives four examples of it.

comprehension.q: In this text, what does rough mean?
comprehension.a: Not flat and not smooth, so your hand feels every part of it.
comprehension.why: The line about the old wall gives the meaning straight after the word.

comprehension.q: What time does the session about metal and plastic start?
comprehension.why: The heading of Session 2 gives the time before the name of the session.

comprehension.q: You are not fond of sitting and listening for an hour. Which session should you not go to?
comprehension.why: Session 3 has no tools, and the notice says you sit and you listen. The student comment says the same thing.

comprehension.q: One person liked Session 2 and still had something bad to say. What was it?
comprehension.a: That it was too short, because one hour is not enough.
comprehension.why: The comment says extremely interesting first, then but, then too short. The word but tells you the opinion turns.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The Thing and the Person
speaking.instructions:
Say each pair out loud. Then record all six lines and play them back.
1. The lesson is interesting. I am interested.
2. The form is confusing. I am confused.
3. The news is exciting. We are excited.
4. The work is tiring. He is tired.
5. The storm was frightening. She was frightened.
6. The journey was boring. I was bored.
Check yourself. In the first half of each pair you say -ing, and you are talking about a thing.
In the second half you say -ed, and you are talking about a person.
If you cannot hear the two endings, say line 1 again slowly, twice.
speaking.tutor: Read me the first half of six pairs, one at a time, and let me say the second half before you tell me the answer.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Did They Like It?
speaking.instructions:
Listen to each line. Say whether that person liked the thing or not, and say how you know.
1. The film was rather slow, and I turned it off after twenty minutes.
2. Session 2 was extremely interesting, but it was too short.
3. I was nervous about coming, and everybody was kind.
4. The talk was slow, and I am not fond of sitting for an hour.
5. The work is hard, but I am keen on getting better at it.
One word in each line carries the opinion.
Find it and say it out loud: slow, interesting, kind, not fond, keen.
Record your five answers and play them back.
Check yourself. Count how many times you named the word that carries the opinion. Four or more is good.
speaking.tutor: Say four short lines about a film, two that like it and two that do not, and let me tell you which is which.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Describe Five Things
speaking.instructions:
Look around you and choose five things. Talk for one minute.
Describe each thing in two sentences.
Sentence 1: how big it is, how old it is, what shape it is, what it is made of.
Sentence 2: how it feels when you touch it.
Model: This is a small old wooden box. It is rough on one side and smooth on the top.
If there is nothing near you, invent the five things.
Record yourself and play it back.
Check yourself. In every first sentence the material word must come last, next to the thing.
speaking.tutor: Listen to my description of five things and tell me only whether my describing words were in the right order.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — What I Think, and Why
speaking.instructions:
Give three opinions out loud. Each one has two parts.
Part 1: what you think. Part 2: why you think it.
Join the two parts with because or with so.
Model: I am not fond of long forms, because the writing is small and confusing.
Model: The shop was quiet all day, so I was bored.
1. An opinion about a film, a book or a song.
2. An opinion about a place you know.
3. An opinion about a kind of work or study.
Made-up opinions are fine.
Record all three and play them back.
Check yourself. Count the reasons. Three opinions need three reasons.
speaking.tutor: Ask me for my opinion about three ordinary things, and after each answer ask me why.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Ask and Answer: What Are You Good At?
speaking.instructions:
This drill has two parts and you take both of them.
Ask the question, wait two seconds, then answer it.
1. What are you good at? Then: I am good at fixing things.
2. What are you interested in? Then: I am interested in old buildings.
3. What are you nervous about? Then: I am nervous about the first day.
4. What are you keen on? Then: I am keen on walking.
5. What are you grateful for? Then: I am grateful for my work.
Now ask and answer the same five with your own answers. Made-up answers are fine.
Record both parts and play them back.
Check yourself. Every answer keeps the small word from its question: at, in, about, on, for.
If somebody is with you, you can ask them the five questions instead and answer theirs back.
speaking.tutor: Ask me five questions with good at, interested in, nervous about, keen on and grateful for, one at a time.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Ninety Seconds About a Day
speaking.instructions:
Speak for ninety seconds about one day. You may invent all of it.
Say six things, in this order.
1. One part of the day that was boring, and how you felt.
2. One part that was interesting, and how you felt.
3. One thing you saw, described with two describing words in front of it.
4. One thing that was too something, or not something enough.
5. One thing you are good at, keen on or grateful for.
6. What you think about that day, with because or so.
Record yourself and play it back.
Check yourself with this list. Six parts. Four sentences with because or so.
Two -ing words about things. Two -ed words about people.
speaking.tutor: After my ninety-second talk, ask me one question about the part of the day I said was boring.

writing.title: Writing 1 — How Much of It
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about a room. You may invent the room.
Use one of these words in each sentence: quite, rather, too, enough, extremely, slightly.
Every sentence says how much of a quality there is.
writing.model:
The room is quite big for one person.
The window is rather small, so the room is dark in the morning.
The shelf is too narrow for my books.
The chair is not high enough for this table.
The floor is extremely cold in the winter.
The door is slightly open all the time.
writing.criteria: Six sentences. Six different words from the list, one in each. Too comes in front of its describing word and enough comes after it.
writing.support: Write the too sentence and the enough sentence first. Put your finger on the describing word, then check which side the word sits on.
writing.extension: Add two more sentences with hardly and almost, about the same room.

writing.title: Writing 2 — The Thing and the Person
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about one day. You may invent the day.
In each sentence, name a thing and then say how a person felt.
Use an -ing word for the thing and an -ed word for the person.
Join the two halves with so.
writing.model:
The journey was tiring, so I was tired all afternoon.
The form was confusing, so we were both confused.
The news was exciting, so she was excited.
The shop was quiet and boring, so I was bored.
The storm was frightening, so the children were frightened.
The lesson was interesting, so everybody was interested.
writing.starter: The journey was tiring, so I was ...
writing.criteria: Six sentences. Every sentence has one -ing word and one -ed word, joined by so. The -ing word sits with the thing and the -ed word sits with the person.
writing.support: Write the six things first, in a list. Then add the person to each one, and only then join them with so.
writing.extension: Write two more sentences with the person first: I was bored, because the shop was quiet and boring.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A Short Review
writing.prompt:
Write a short review of a film, a book, a shop or a place. You may invent it.
Five sentences. Say what you think and how it made you feel.
Give at least two reasons, with because or so.
Use one -ing word, one -ed word and one word from the How much of it group.
writing.model:
I watched a film last night and it was rather slow.
The first twenty minutes were interesting, because nobody said very much.
After that nothing happened, so I was bored.
The last part was extremely good, but it came too late for me.
I am not keen on long films, and this one was not short enough.
writing.starter: I watched a film last night and it was ...
writing.criteria: Five sentences. Two reasons with because or so. One -ing word, one -ed word, one word from the How much of it group. Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Say the five sentences out loud first, then write down exactly what you said. Start with what you think, and add the reason after because.
writing.extension: Write one more sentence that says who would like it and who would not.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A Comment for the Notice Board
writing.prompt:
Write a comment like the ones at the foot of the library notice.
You went to one of the three sessions. You may invent everything.
Four sentences.
Say how you felt before, what the session was like, what was not good, and what you will do next time.
Do not use your real name. Write your role at the end, like this: From a driver.
writing.model:
I was nervous about coming, because I am not good at making things.
Session 1 was quiet and extremely interesting.
The hour was too short, and I did not finish my box.
I am keen on coming again, and next time I will bring a smaller one.
From a nurse.
writing.starter: I was nervous about coming, because ...
writing.criteria: Four sentences and a role at the end. One sentence says how you felt, with an -ed word. One sentence says what the thing was like, with an -ing word. One reason with because or so. No real name.
writing.support: Read the three comments on the notice again. Copy the shape of the one you like best, and change every fact in it.
writing.extension: Write a second comment from somebody who did not like the same session, and give their reason.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Boring or Bored
activities.instructions:
Write the right word in each gap.
1. The journey was long and slow, so I was ... (boring, bored).
2. That book is ... (interesting, interested). I read it twice.
3. She is ... (exciting, excited) about the new job.
4. The map was ... (confusing, confused), so we asked at the shop.
5. I am ... (interesting, interested) in old buildings.
6. The storm last night was ... (frightening, frightened).
7. He works twelve hours a day, so he is always ... (tiring, tired).
8. Small writing on a long form is ... (confusing, confused).
activities.answers:
1. bored  2. interesting  3. excited  4. confusing  5. interested  6. frightening  7. tired  8. confusing
Eight out of eight means you have it.
Six or seven means check the two you missed. Ask one question of each gap: is this word about a thing, or about a person?
Five or fewer means read Pattern 1 again before you go on.
activities.solo: Cover the answers with your hand. Write all eight, then move your hand and mark them yourself.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Put Them in Order
activities.instructions:
Put the describing words in the right order in front of the thing.
1. (plastic, small) a ... bottle
2. (metal, round, big) a ... tray
3. (wooden, old, narrow) a ... shelf
4. (white, square, large) a ... card
5. (new, shiny, metal) a ... spoon
6. (plastic, green, small) a ... bowl
7. (round, wooden, small) a ... table
8. (narrow, long, metal) a ... box
activities.answers:
1. a small plastic bottle  2. a big round metal tray  3. a narrow old wooden shelf  4. a large square white card
5. a shiny new metal spoon  6. a small green plastic bowl  7. a small round wooden table  8. a long narrow metal box
Item 4 is the one people miss. Shape comes before colour, so square goes in front of white.
Item 5 is the other hard one. Shiny is not a size, an age, a shape or a colour, so it goes in front of all of them.
Six or more out of eight is a pass. Five or fewer means read Pattern 2 again.
activities.solo: Read each finished phrase out loud. A wrong order sounds wrong before you can name the rule.

activities.title: Practice 3 — How Much of It
activities.instructions:
Choose the right word for each gap.
1. The soup is (quite, too) hot to eat. I will wait ten minutes.
2. I (hardly, almost) slept last night, so I am very tired today.
3. The work is (almost, completely) finished. One box is still open.
4. The bottle is (slightly, extremely) heavy. I can carry it easily.
5. The glass is (rather, hardly) dirty. Please wash it again.
6. The room is not warm (enough, too).
7. The bottle is (completely, slightly) empty. There is nothing in it.
8. The shop is (quite, too) near. It takes me five minutes to walk there.
activities.answers:
1. too  2. hardly  3. almost  4. slightly  5. rather  6. enough  7. completely  8. quite
Item 8 is the one people miss. Too near would mean the shop is nearer than you want, and five minutes is a good amount, so the word is quite.
Item 4 catches people too. You can carry it easily, so it is only slightly heavy.
Six or more out of eight is a pass. Five or fewer means read Pattern 3 again.
activities.solo: Read the second sentence of each item first. The second sentence always tells you how much there is.

activities.title: Practice 4 — The Small Word
activities.instructions:
Write at, in, of, on, for, about or with in each gap.
1. I am not aware ... any change in the time.
2. She is curious ... the new shop on the corner.
3. He is very good ... numbers.
4. They are keen ... walking in the morning.
5. I am grateful ... your help.
6. Do not be impatient ... yourself.
7. I am fond ... that old wooden chair.
8. Are you interested ... this kind of work?
activities.answers:
1. of  2. about  3. at  4. on  5. for  6. with  7. of  8. in
Eight out of eight means you have it.
Three of them take of: aware, fond and ashamed. Learn those three together.
Item 3 is the one people miss. Good always brings at, never in.
Six or seven means write the pairs in a list and say them out loud twice. Five or fewer means read Pattern 4 again.
activities.solo: Cover the answers. Say each whole sentence out loud before you write the small word, because your ear often knows it first.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Match the Word to Its Meaning
activities.instructions:
Match each word to its meaning. Write the number and the letter.
1. hardly
2. rather
3. shiny
4. ashamed
5. narrow
6. grateful
7. completely
8. rough
a. bright, because the light comes back off it
b. all of it, with nothing left
c. almost not at all
d. not smooth, so your hand feels every part of it
e. feeling thanks to somebody who helped you
f. more than you want, or more than you expected
g. not wide, only a short way from one side to the other
h. feeling bad about something you did
activities.answers:
1c  2f  3a  4h  5g  6e  7b  8d
Eight out of eight is a pass.
The pair people swap is 1 and 7. Hardly means almost none. Completely means all of it. They are the two ends of the same line.
Six or seven means read the word cards again, then try it a second time on another day.
activities.solo: Cover the letters with a piece of paper. Say each meaning from memory first, then move the paper and check.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Find It on the Notice Board
activities.instructions:
Read the library notice board again. Answer each question and say which part it comes from.
1. How long is one session?
2. Which session has no tools in it?
3. What should you bring to Session 1?
4. Why is the room not large enough for a big table?
5. On which days can you call, and between which times?
6. Which two people wrote something good and something bad in the same comment?
activities.answers:
1. One hour, from the line under the heading.
2. Session 3, the talk at 14.00.
3. An old wooden chair or a small wooden box, from Session 1.
4. The notice does not say why. It only says the room is not large enough, under WHAT TO BRING.
5. Monday to Friday, from 10 until 4, under TO ASK A QUESTION.
6. The driver and the student. The driver says extremely interesting but too short. The student says bored but my friend loved it.
Five or six out of six is a pass. Item 4 is the one people miss, because a notice often gives a fact and no reason. Saying that the notice does not say is the right answer.
activities.solo: Put your finger on the heading of each part before you look for the answer. The headings tell you where to look.

options: The journey was long, so I was bored.
The journey was long, so I was boring.
The journey was long, so it was bored.
The journey was long, so I am boring it.
quizzes.a: The journey was long, so I was bored.
quizzes.why: I is a person, so the word is bored. I was boring says that other people were bored with you, which is not the meaning here. The journey is a thing, so it can be boring but never bored.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: The form had six pages and very small writing. It was ... .
quizzes.why: The form is a thing, so it takes the -ing word. Confused is for the person who reads it. Confuse is the verb on its own, and confusingly says how somebody does something.

quizzes.q: Which one puts the describing words in the order English uses?
quizzes.why: Size comes first, then age, then what it is made of. The two options that begin with wooden put the material first, and the material always goes last. The option that begins with old puts age before size.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: This shelf is not wide ... for the box.
quizzes.why: Enough comes after the describing word, and not wide enough means there is less width than you need. Too would have to come in front of wide, not after it. Very and quite say how much there is and do not fit after not wide.

quizzes.q: Which sentence means you could not drink the tea?
quizzes.why: Too means more than you can use, so you cannot drink it. Quite hot is a good amount and hot enough means it has reached what you need. Slightly hot means only a very little heat.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: She is very good ... numbers.
quizzes.why: Good always brings at with it, and the pair never changes. Good in is the commonest wrong answer, because many languages join the two words another way. Good for means healthy or useful, and good with is used about people or animals, not about a skill like this.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: I am nervous ... the test tomorrow.
quizzes.why: Nervous brings about. Afraid is the word that brings of, so nervous of is a mix of two pairs. For goes with grateful and ready, and at goes with good and bad.

quizzes.q: Which word means almost not at all?
quizzes.why: Hardly means there is almost none of the thing: I hardly slept. Completely is the other end of the line, and means all of it. Extremely means a very great amount, and rather means more than you wanted.

options: I am interested in old buildings.
I am interesting in old buildings.
I am interested of old buildings.
I am interest in old buildings.
quizzes.a: I am interested in old buildings.
quizzes.why: I is a person, so the word is interested, and interested always brings in. Interesting would describe the buildings, not you. Of belongs with fond and aware, and interest on its own is not a describing word.

quizzes.q: On the library notice board, which session has no tools in it?
quizzes.why: The Session 3 lines say there are no tools and that you sit and you listen. Sessions 1 and 2 both ask you to bring a thing to work on, and the notice says the tools are all there.

quizzes.q: One comment says Session 2 was extremely interesting, but too short. What is that person telling you?
options: They did not go to Session 2.
They liked it and wanted more time.
The session was at the wrong time of day.
quizzes.a: They liked it and wanted more time.
quizzes.why: Extremely interesting is the good half, and too short means there was less time than they wanted. The word but joins the two halves. Too short is the opposite of long, and nothing in the comment is about the time of day or about not going.

quizzes.q: Choose the right word: The work is ... finished. One box is still open.
quizzes.why: One box is still open, so the work is very near the end but not all the way there. Completely finished would mean nothing is left. Hardly finished would mean almost none of it is done, and extremely does not go with finished at all.

teacherNotes.note: The error this unit exists for is I am boring for I am bored. It is not a vocabulary gap: the learner knows both words and has chosen the wrong one, because in many languages one form covers both jobs. Do not correct it by naming a participle. Ask the learner to point at the word in front of the -ing or -ed word in the model line, then to point at the same place in their own sentence. If that word is a person, the ending has to be -ed. The learner can then run the same test alone on every sentence they write.

In Speaking 2 the learner has to hear the word that carries the opinion, not the whole line. If they answer the wrong way round, read the line again and stop just before the opinion word, so that they finish it themselves. This is a listening difficulty before it is a grammar one, and going back to the grammar card will not fix it.

Practice 3 item 8 is the hardest item in the unit, and it is worth going back to if the learner misses it. The shop is five minutes away, which is a good amount of near, so the word is quite. Too near would mean nearer than the learner wants, which is a real thing to say about a loud road but not about a shop. Too always carries a problem with it, and quite does not. If the learner cannot hear that, ask them what is wrong in the sentence. If nothing is wrong, the word is not too.

Nothing in this unit asks the learner to say what frightens them, what they are ashamed of or what they are nervous about in their own life. Every task with feelings in it says that made-up answers are fine, and Writing 4 asks for a role rather than a name. If a learner volunteers something real, keep the work on the English.

A learner who finishes early can take Reading 2 and rewrite three of its descriptions with a different material and a different size. A learner who is struggling should do Pattern 1 and Practice 1 twice, on two different days, before going on to Pattern 2. The four patterns here are independent of one another, so a learner can hold one back without blocking the rest of the unit.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say that a thing was boring and that I was bored.
I can describe a thing and put the describing words in the right order.
I can say that something is quite big, rather slow or not warm enough.
I can say good at, interested in and afraid of with the right small word.
I can give an opinion out loud and a reason for it.
I can find what the writer of a short text or a notice thinks.
I can write four or five sentences about what I think and how I feel.
I can hear whether somebody liked a thing or not.

assignment.title: Boring or Bored: a spoken review and a written comment
assignment.instructions:
This assignment has two parts. You may invent every fact in it.

Part 1, spoken.
Record ninety seconds about something you did: a film, a journey, a job or a day out.
Say what the thing was like, with two -ing words.
Say how you felt, with two -ed words.
Describe one object you saw, with two describing words in front of it.
Say how much of one quality there was, with quite, rather, too or enough.
End with your opinion and a reason for it, joined by because or so.

Part 2, written.
Write a four-sentence comment about the same thing, for a notice board.
One sentence says how you felt before it.
One sentence says what it was like.
One sentence says what was not good enough.
One sentence says what you will do next time.
End with a role, not a name, like this: From a driver.

Before you send it, play your recording back once and read your comment out loud.
Fix anything you hear that is wrong.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written comment
